chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Ahmad ibn Muhammad altogether, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Rafa'ah al-Nakhhas, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), so I said, 'I bargained with a man for a slave girl of his, and he sold her to me with my option (hukm). So I took possession of her from him upon that. Then I sent to him a thousand dirhams and said to him, 'This thousand is my option upon you.' But he refused to accept it from me, and I had already touched her before I sent to him the thousand dirhams.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'I view that you should evaluate the slave girl with a fair price. So if her price was more than what you sent to him, it is upon you to return to him what was deficient from the price; and if her price was less than what you sent to him, then it is for him.'

He said: 'I said, 'What is your view if I find a defect in her after having touched her?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not for you to return her, and for you is to take the value of what is between the health and the defect.'

key_terms.حُكْمِي: My option (a right to accept or reject a sale within a specified period)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on a sale with an option (hukm) when the buyer inspects the goods and finds a defect?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia juristic approach to conditional sales (bay' al-hukm), emphasizing the necessity of fair valuation (taqyim) to resolve discrepancies between the initial payment and the agreed price. It further clarifies the distinction between inspection (tamass) and defect (ayb), ruling that post-inspection defects warrant a price deduction rather than rescission of the contract, reflecting the principle of fairness in commercial transactions.
